title: India's EV Market Grew 81 Per Cent Last Year. Tesla Sold 35 Cars Last Month.
excerpt: Tata doubled its electric car sales, Mahindra doubled too, Maruti entered with 1,591 units — and India just told Tesla it can either build a factory or keep its showrooms.
body:
India sold 26,682 electric cars in May 2026. Tesla accounted for 35 of them.

That single data point, buried in monthly registration figures published this week, tells the story of an EV market that is booming on Indian terms and largely ignoring the world's most famous electric car company. Year-on-year, India's electric passenger car segment grew 81.2 per cent in May, adding 11,957 units over May 2025's tally of 14,725.

The market leader is not a Silicon Valley disruptor. It is Tata Motors, which sold 10,340 electric cars in May — more than double its 5,083 a year earlier — and now commands 38.75 per cent of the market. Mahindra followed with 6,210 units, up 114.8 per cent year-on-year, holding 23.27 per cent. JSW MG sold 4,984, and Maruti Suzuki — India's largest automaker by combustion vehicle sales — entered the EV segment with 1,591 units in what is effectively its debut month.

Even Vietnam's VinFast outsold Tesla in India, moving 1,238 units. China's BYD sold 686.

## Tesla's India Problem

Tesla's negligible presence in the data is not an accident. It is the result of a deliberate standoff between the company and the Indian government.

India this week notified final operational guidelines for its flagship EV manufacturing scheme, which cuts import duties to 15 per cent from a staggering 110 per cent for electric vehicles with a cost, insurance, and freight value of $35,000 or more — but only if the manufacturer commits to investing at least ₹4,150 crore to establish a production facility within three years.

Heavy Industries Minister H.D. Kumaraswamy spelled it out at a press conference. Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen-Skoda, and Hyundai have all shown interest in manufacturing in India. "Tesla," he said, "only wants to start two showrooms. They are not interested in manufacturing in India."

The policy is India's way of saying: build here or pay full freight. Tesla, which entered the Indian market late and has priced its Model Y starting at over ₹63 lakh, has so far declined to commit to local production. At 35 units a month — down from 43 in April — it is outsold by BMW (352 units), Kia (349), and even Mercedes-Benz (208).

## The Homegrown Surge

The real action is in the sub-₹20 lakh segment, where Tata's Nexon EV and Punch EV, Mahindra's XUV400 and BE 6, and MG's ZS EV compete for the mainstream Indian buyer.

India's EV growth has been running above 80 per cent year-on-year for the entire fiscal year. FY26 collectively clocked 83.63 per cent growth, and the trajectory has survived the Middle East conflict, which pushed input costs higher across the automotive supply chain. Tata Motors announced a price hike of up to 1.5 per cent across its passenger vehicle range — including EVs — from July 1. Maruti Suzuki and Hyundai have already raised prices.

The cost pressures are real. Rising crude prices have elevated the cost of steel, aluminium, and petrochemical-derived components. Tata Motors said the increase was aimed at "partially offsetting rising input costs and sustained inflationary pressures."

But the demand curve has held. The government's PM E-DRIVE scheme continues to subsidise electric two-wheelers through July 2026 and electric three-wheelers through March 2028. Delhi's new draft EV policy offers 100 per cent road tax and registration fee exemptions for electric cars priced up to ₹30 lakh — a ceiling that captures the entire mainstream EV segment while pointedly excluding Tesla's Model Y.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI investors and families, the Indian EV market represents one of the few bright spots in a year otherwise dominated by geopolitical anxiety and capital flight. Tata Motors' EV business has gone from a curiosity to a serious revenue stream, and Mahindra's Born Electric range has made it a credible second force.

The question is whether India can build the charging infrastructure fast enough to sustain 80 per cent annual growth. The government's policy architecture — favourable import duties for manufacturers who invest locally, aggressive state-level incentives, and subsidy extensions — is designed to attract the global supply chain to India rather than just its consumers.

Tesla's 35-car month is a reminder that in India, showing up with a premium product and no factory is not a strategy. It is a rounding error.

nri_angle: For NRIs considering an EV for family in India or tracking the Indian market for investment, the numbers are clear — India's EV revolution is being built by homegrown brands, and Tesla is barely a footnote.
